editorial_work_list.description: You’re receiving this notification because one or more Azure subscriptions associated with your account use Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images. You can also find this notification in the Azure portal under Service Health > Health advisories (https://aka.ms/AzureServiceHealthAdvisories) by using tracking ID 8PJS-_48. In October 2024, we announced upcoming changes to Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images (https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azurecompute/incoming-changes-for-window-server-2022-marketplace-image-users/4262423). On 14 July 2026, we deprecated images preinstalled with .NET 6 because .NET 6 had reached the end of support. To avoid disruptions, migrate any affected SKUs listed below to supported Windows Server 2022 images. Use the new offer ID (Offer ID) provided in the linked announcement. 2022-DATACENTER 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-CORE 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-G2 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK-G2 2022-DATACENTER-G2 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK-G2 Recommended action To avoid disruptions, migrate affected workloads to supported Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images now. Review the .NET 6 image migration guidance (https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azurecompute/incoming-changes-for-window-server-2022-marketplace-image-users/4262423) to learn how to identify affected images in your subscriptions, complete the migration, and locate the replacement images. Help and support If you have questions or encounter issues related to the end of support for .NET 6 or migration to a supported version, visit the Services Hub (https://support.serviceshub.microsoft.com/supportforbusiness/onboarding?origin=/supportforbusiness/create) or create an Azure support request (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-portal/supportability/how-to-create-azure-support-request). When creating the request, select the product family Developer Tools, the product .NET, and the version .NET 10.

To stay within supported versions and service-level agreements (SLA), upgrade to a supported version within 30 days after Azure removes version 1.34 Kubernetes Official version

Resources 
| where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' 
| extend props = todynamic(properties) 
| mv-expand ap = props.agentPoolProfiles 
| extend currentOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend requestedOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.orchestratorVersion) 
| extend orchestratorVersion = iff( 
    isempty(currentOrchestratorVersion),

| project subscriptionId, id

actions.description: Upgrade AKS cluster to a supported Long Term Support Version

3afd0e0e-36bd-444b-97d7-d1e85d44066d.detailedDescription: Azure Kubernetes Service retires 1.30 LTS version. To stay within supported versions and service-level agreements (SLA), upgrade to a supported version within 30 days after Azure removes version 1.30 LTS.

3afd0e0e-36bd-444b-97d7-d1e85d44066d.recommendationDataSourceQuery:
Resources
 | where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters'
 | extend props = todynamic(properties)
 | mv-expand ap = props.agentPoolProfiles
 | extend currentOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.currentOrchestratorVersion)
 | extend requestedOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.orchestratorVersion)
 | extend orchestratorVersion = iff(isempty(currentOrchestratorVersion), requestedOrchestratorVersion,
 currentOrchestratorVersion)
 | where orchestratorVersion == '1.30' or orchestratorVersion startswith '1.30.'
 | project subscriptionId, id

actions.caption: Change disk type
actions.description: Change disk type

3c03549b-9c0a-4c13-bed4-def3c7e34ddd.detailedDescription: HDD operating system (OS) disks are being retired in September 2028. Upgrade the OS disk from Standard HDD to Standard SSD for increased uptime of single-instance virtual machine and improved input/output operations and throughput.
3c03549b-9c0a-4c13-bed4-def3c7e34ddd.displayName: Upgrade to Standard SSD OS disk
3c03549b-9c0a-4c13-bed4-def3c7e34ddd.label: Upgrade to Standard SSD OS disk
3c03549b-9c0a-4c13-bed4-def3c7e34ddd.potentialBenefits: Boost single-instance VM uptime from 95% to 99.5%.
3c03549b-9c0a-4c13-bed4-def3c7e34ddd.recommendationDataSourceQuery:
resources
| where type =~ 'Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines'  
| extend provisioningState = tostring(properties.provisioningState)  
| extend creationTime = todatetime(properties.timeCreated)
| extend osDiskSKU = tostring(properties.storageProfile.osDisk.managedDisk.storageAccountType)
| extend isEphemeral = tostring(properties.storageProfile.osDisk.diffDiskSettings)
| extend runningState = tostring(properties.extended.instanceView.powerState.displayStatus)
| where provisioningState == "Succeeded"
| where osDiskSKU == "Standard_LRS"
| where isempty(isEphemeral)
| where creationTime < ago(7d) and creationTime > ago(8d)
| project subscriptionId, id

Resources 
| where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' 
| extend props = todynamic(properties) 
| mv-expand ap = props.agentPoolProfiles 
| extend currentOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend requestedOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.orchestratorVersion) 
| extend orchestratorVersion = iff( 
    isempty(currentOrchestratorVersion), 
    requestedOrchestratorVersion, 
    currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend supportPlan = tostring(props.supportPlan) 
| where (orchestratorVersion == '1.33'

| where supportPlan =~ 'AKSLongTermSupport' 
| project subscriptionId, id

actions.caption: Upgrade AKS cluster from 1.32 Kubernetes official version
actions.description: Upgrade AKS cluster from 1.32 Kubernetes official version

7dcef62e-792c-49dc-b36a-1938829c449c.detailedDescription: Azure Kubernetes Service retires 1.32 Kubernetes Official version. To stay within supported versions and service-level agreements (SLA), upgrade to a supported version within 30 days after Azure removes version 1.32 Kubernetes Official version
7dcef62e-792c-49dc-b36a-1938829c449c.displayName: Upgrade your AKS cluster from 1.32 Kubernetes Official version
7dcef62e-792c-49dc-b36a-1938829c449c.label: Upgrade your AKS cluster from 1.32 Kubernetes Official version
7dcef62e-792c-49dc-b36a-1938829c449c.recommendationDataSourceQuery:
Resources 
| where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' 
| extend props = todynamic(properties) 
| mv-expand ap = props.agentPoolProfiles 
| extend currentOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend requestedOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.orchestratorVersion) 
| extend orchestratorVersion = iff( 
    isempty(currentOrchestratorVersion), 
    requestedOrchestratorVersion, 
    currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend supportPlan = tostring(props.supportPlan) 
| where (orchestratorVersion == '1.32' 
    or orchestratorVersion startswith '1.32.') 
| where supportPlan =~ 'KubernetesOfficial' 
| project subscriptionId, id

997ec7aa-2f8d-4268-9ac0-4e8147cbe9d7.recommendationDataSourceQuery:
Resources 
| where type =~ 'microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' 
| extend props = todynamic(properties) 
| mv-expand ap = props.agentPoolProfiles 
| extend currentOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend requestedOrchestratorVersion = tostring(ap.orchestratorVersion) 
| extend orchestratorVersion = iff( 
    isempty(currentOrchestratorVersion), 
    requestedOrchestratorVersion, 
    currentOrchestratorVersion) 
| extend supportPlan = tostring(props.supportPlan) 
| where (orchestratorVersion == '1.34' 
    or orchestratorVersion startswith '1.34.') 
| where supportPlan =~ 'AKSLongTermSupport' 
| project subscriptionId, id

items.description: You’re receiving this notification because one or more Azure subscriptions associated with your account use Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images. You can also find this notification in the Azure portal under Service Health > Health advisories (https://aka.ms/AzureServiceHealthAdvisories) by using tracking ID 8PJS-_48. In October 2024, we announced upcoming changes to Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images (https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azurecompute/incoming-changes-for-window-server-2022-marketplace-image-users/4262423). On 14 July 2026, we deprecated images preinstalled with .NET 6 because .NET 6 had reached the end of support. To avoid disruptions, migrate any affected SKUs listed below to supported Windows Server 2022 images. Use the new offer ID (Offer ID) provided in the linked announcement. 2022-DATACENTER 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-CORE 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-G2 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK-G2 2022-DATACENTER-G2 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK-G2 Recommended action To avoid disruptions, migrate affected workloads to supported Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images now. Review the .NET 6 image migration guidance (https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azurecompute/incoming-changes-for-window-server-2022-marketplace-image-users/4262423) to learn how to identify affected images in your subscriptions, complete the migration, and locate the replacement images. Help and support If you have questions or encounter issues related to the end of support for .NET 6 or migration to a supported version, visit the Services Hub (https://support.serviceshub.microsoft.com/supportforbusiness/onboarding?origin=/supportforbusiness/create) or create an Azure support request (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-portal/supportability/how-to-create-azure-support-request). When creating the request, select the product family Developer Tools, the product .NET, and the version .NET 10.
items.title: Migrate from deprecated Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images to supported images now to avoid service disruptions

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.

  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments.

What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.

  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments.

Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026)

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful? 

  • There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident. 
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF

  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues – by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026)

properties.description:
This notification is for upcoming scheduled maintenance to your Azure App Service instance(s) in the Italy North region. Actual upgrade operations will start after 7pm local time in region. Maintenance is optimized for non-business hours of a given region. During this maintenance, your Azure App Service application(s) may see a brief drop in connectivity for a few seconds. Please see frequently asked questions for maintenance notifications: Routine maintenance for App Service. For maximum availability and minimal disruption to your service, follow our list of best practices outlined here: The Ultimate Guide to Running Healthy Apps in the Cloud. Feel free to refer to your Azure portal for more information, FAQs regarding routine maintenance notifications, and for any additional questions, please contact support. Release Notes Release - Azure/AppService
To view your resource list in the region, click here. The resource list with maintenance status is now also available within Impacted Resources tab of this event from Service Health.

Maintenance is optimized for non-business hours of a given region. During this maintenance, your Azure App Service application(s) may see a brief drop in connectivity for a few seconds. Please see frequently asked questions for maintenance notifications: Routine maintenance for App Service. For maximum availability and minimal disruption to your service, follow our list of best practices outlined here: The Ultimate Guide to Running Healthy Apps in the Cloud. Feel free to refer to your Azure portal for more information, FAQs regarding routine maintenance notifications, and for any additional questions, please contact support. Release Notes Release - Azure/AppService
To view your resource list in the region, click here. The resource list with maintenance status is now also available within Impacted Resources tab of this event from Service Health.

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful? 

  • There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident. 
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration, so are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact to service availability varied between customers and resources – for guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring 
  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues – by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts 

How can we make our incident communications more useful? 

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: Customer feedback survey (8Q1S-GLG)

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful? 

  • There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident. 
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration, so are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact to service availability varied between customers and resources – for guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring 
  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues – by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts 

How can we make our incident communications more useful? 

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: Customer feedback survey (8Q1S-GLG)

In October 2024, we announced upcoming changes to Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images. On 14 July 2026, we deprecated images preinstalled with .NET 6 because .NET 6 had reached the end of support. To avoid disruptions, migrate any affected SKUs listed below to supported Windows Server 2022 images. Use the new offer ID (Offer ID) provided in the linked announcement.

To avoid disruptions, migrate affected workloads to supported Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images now. Review the .NET 6 image migration guidance to learn how to identify affected images in your subscriptions, complete the migration, and locate the replacement images.

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful? 

  • There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident. 
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration, so are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact to service availability varied between customers and resources – for guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring 
  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues – by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts 

How can we make our incident communications more useful? 

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: Customer feedback survey (8Q1S-GLG)

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.

  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments.

You’re receiving this notification because one or more Azure subscriptions associated with your account use Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images. You can also find this notification in the Azure portal under Service Health > Health advisories by using tracking ID 8PJS-_48. 

In October 2024, we announced upcoming changes to Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images. On 14 July 2026, we deprecated images preinstalled with .NET 6 because .NET 6 had reached the end of support. To avoid disruptions, migrate any affected SKUs listed below to supported Windows Server 2022 images. Use the new offer ID (Offer ID) provided in the linked announcement. 

  • 2022-DATACENTER 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-CORE-SMALLDISK 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-HOTPATCH-SMALLDISK 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-AZURE-EDITION-SMALLDISK 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-CORE 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-G2 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-CORE-SMALLDISK-G2 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-G2 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK 
  • 2022-DATACENTER-SMALLDISK-G2 

Recommended action 

To avoid disruptions, migrate affected workloads to supported Microsoft Marketplace Windows Server 2022 images now. Review the .NET 6 image migration guidance to learn how to identify affected images in your subscriptions, complete the migration, and locate the replacement images. 

Help and support 

If you have questions or encounter issues related to the end of support for .NET 6 or migration to a supported version, visit the Services Hub or create an Azure support request. When creating the request, select the product family Developer Tools, the product .NET, and the version .NET 10.

What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.

  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments.

properties.description:
What happened? 

Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.   

What went wrong, and why? 

We determined that a recently introduced update to a security-related platform component, the Azure Security Agent (ASA), contributed to periodic increases in CPU utilization on Redis infrastructure. During scheduled background security scanning activities, log processing by ASA processes consumed additional system resources, leaving fewer resources available for Redis workloads. This resulted in increased latency and command timeouts for a subset of customer workloads. The affected ASA version was introduced through an automated platform deployment process and was applied broadly across the environment. The impact was more pronounced for workloads running on smaller virtual machines because they had fewer processing resources available to handle the additional activity generated by the security scanning processes. 

How did we respond? 

  • 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.  
  • 10:11 UTC on 2 September 2026 – We became aware of the issue through customer reports and began investigating. 
  • 02:45 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We identified a correlation between recurring CPU utilization increases and scheduled security scanning activities associated with the updated component.  
  • 18:58 UTC on 3 September 2026 – We began testing a rollback in test environments to evaluate its effectiveness and potential impact.  
  • 17:31 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We identified the specific process within the security component that was contributing to the increased system load.  
  • 18:25 UTC on 4 September 2026 – We expanded rollback testing to targeted production environments to gather additional data and validate the mitigation.  
  • 15:21 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Based on the results of the rollback testing, we confirmed that the rollback was safe and that the issue no longer reproduced.  
  • 17:46 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We confirmed that the issue had affected multiple environments and began coordinating mitigation across the affected infrastructure.  
  • 21:15 UTC on 8 September 2026 – We implemented mitigation actions, including disabling the affected scanning activity and reverting the security component to the previous version.  
  • 23:50 UTC on 8 September 2026 – Service was restored and customer impact was mitigated after we validated the mitigation and completed the rollout across affected environments. 

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? 

  • We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 
  • We are improving process efficiency and evaluating additional resiliency safeguards to reduce the impact of scheduled security scanning activity on service performance. (Estimated completion: November 2026) 

How can customers make incidents like this less impactful? 

  • There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident. 
  • More generally, consider evaluating the reliability of your applications using guidance from the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its interactive Well-Architected Review: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/WAF 
  • The impact times above represent the full incident duration, so are not specific to any individual customer. Actual impact to service availability varied between customers and resources – for guidance on implementing monitoring to understand granular impact: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Monitoring 
  • Finally, consider ensuring that the right people in your organization will be notified about any future service issues – by configuring Azure Service Health alerts. These can trigger emails, SMS, push notifications, webhooks, and more: https://aka.ms/AzPIR/Alerts 

How can we make our incident communications more useful? 

You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: Customer feedback survey (8Q1S-GLG)
